newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Mining industry relieved over end to Busang saga.
newsitem.headline: Mining industry relieved over end to Busang saga.

text.p: Mining industry sources expressed relief on Tuesday that the end of the long-running Busang gold saga was in sight, but analysts said questions remained over the development of one of the world's richest gold finds.
Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana announced government approval of a plan by Canada's small Bre-X Minerals Ltd mining company to develop Busang.

Bre-X, which uncovered the motherlode it estimates to contain at least 71 million ounces of gold on Borneo island, is to get a 45 percent stake in the richest area, Indonesian partners and the government 40 percent and the U.S. giant Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc 15 percent.
A marriage at government behest between Bre-X and Canada's Barrick Gold Corp dissolved before consummation.
Freeport, which operates one of the world's biggest copper and gold mines in Indonesia's Irian Jaya province, will develop and run the Busang operation.
"It's certainly been a long drawn-out drama," one leading industry source said.
"It'll be nice to put it behind us and get on with exploration and mining under the contract of work system that has worked so well for so many years," he added.

The international mining industry had expressed growing concern over the way in which the government appeared to be ignoring the contract of work system and forcing Bre-X into the arms of Barrick, apparently at the behest of powerful local interests.

The appearance of members of President Suharto's family in the tortuous tale also complicated matters, causing concern in the business community that doing deals in Indonesia could become even more complicated.
A top official of the Mines and Energy Ministry, Kuntoro Mangkusubroto, the respected director general of mines, moved on Tuesday to allay concerns.
"The Busang case will not change the government's general mining policy, for the time being at least," he told a news conference. "The Busang case is a specific one."

He said the government would move soon to approve 68 outstanding contracts of work (COWS) expected last year and which are needed by foreign firms and their local partners to explore and develop properties.

"I think the government needs to move quickly to approve the backlog of COWS. Nothing will be more positive for the industry than to get back to work and stick to the contract of work system," one mining official said.
"That's the most positive thing they can do," he added.
"The jury is still out," said Laurie Fitzgerald. mining analyst for brokerage Hartley Poynton of Perth, Australia.
"If the end result satisfies all of the conditions of the Indonesian government up front in terms of the contract of work, you would have to say it (the Busang turmoil) is all over.
"In the past, the contract of work in Indonesia has been as good as gold," he said.

Industry sources said Freeport McMoRan was expected to move quickly with Bre-X to settle legal details, make environmental, geological and engineering assessments and get preparations under way to develop Busang.
"There is still a lot of infrastructure work to be done...Busang is in a very remote location," noted Keith Goode, mining analyst for Australia's Bell Securities Ltd.
